Hi there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Dr. Ramirez, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician here. I specialize in caring for new mothers, and I’m glad we have this time together.

To get a quick, clear picture of how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us pick up on symptoms of depression or anxiety that can creep up in the postpartum year, and it includes a question about self-harm so we can keep you safe. Nothing we discuss today goes beyond this room unless you or your baby’s safety is at risk, so please feel free to speak openly.

We’ll walk through 10 questions about how you’ve felt in the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can ask me to repeat or re-word anything.

Ready to begin?

In the past week, have you still been able to look forward with enjoyment to things—like seeing a friend, having a favorite snack, or getting out for a short walk—or has even pleasant stuff felt kind of blah or pointless?

[soft voice, slow to respond]

I… I guess I still try to meet a friend for coffee, or I’ll sit outside for a few minutes when the sun’s out. I tell myself I should enjoy it, but most of the time it feels… flat, like I’m just going through the motions. It’s not completely pointless, but it’s nowhere near the lift it used to give me.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[half-shrug, eyes on the floor]

I still laugh sometimes—like when my husband makes a dumb joke or when the baby does something goofy—but it feels kind of forced. Most of the time the humor just doesn’t land the way it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[quiet sigh]

Honestly, I don’t really look forward to much anymore. I’ll tell myself, “It’ll be nice to get out,” but when the time comes, it just feels like another chore. Even little treats I used to like feel kind of empty now.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes tear up a little]

Yeah… I keep thinking if I were just more organized or patient, the baby wouldn’t be so fussy at night. When anything goes wrong—like when she won’t settle—I immediately wonder what I did wrong, even if it’s not really my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrapping my cardigan tighter]

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly worry her breathing sounds different, or I’ll lie awake imagining she’ll choke when I’m not looking. There’s no real reason—it’s just this constant buzz of “what if something happens?”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes it hits me out of nowhere—like my heart’s racing and I can’t catch my breath. I’ll be folding laundry or just walking to the kitchen, and suddenly I’m sure something awful is about to happen, even though nothing’s wrong.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like the minute I finish one thing—feeding, changing, pumping—there’s another pile of laundry or dishes or a text I forgot to answer. I keep telling myself I just need to push through, but sometimes I end up crying while I’m folding onesies because it all feels like too much.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[looking down, voice low]

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop. I replay everything I think I did wrong that day—did I hold her enough, did I miss a feeding cue, am I already failing her? It takes me a long time to drift off, and when I finally do, I wake up after a couple of hours with my heart pounding for no clear reason.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad most of the day. It’s like there’s this heavy blanket over everything. I can still smile for the baby or answer when someone talks to me, but inside it just feels… gray, and sometimes I end up crying when I’m alone because it feels like it’ll never lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[voice cracks, eyes watering]

Yeah… it’s usually at night after I’ve finally gotten her down. I’ll sit in the rocking chair and just start crying—sometimes quietly, sometimes really hard. It feels like the sadness just spills out and I can’t stop it, even when I tell myself I should be grateful.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[long pause, eyes fixed on my hands]

I… I have had a couple of quick flashes this week—like “what if I just didn’t wake up” or “maybe if I got hurt I could rest in the hospital.” They’re only thoughts, no plan or anything, but they scared me enough that I pushed them away fast.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: POSTPARTUM MOOD & ANXIETY SCREENING SUMMARY – EPDS analogue

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily crying spells  
- Marked guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Generalized anxiety, panic surges, intrusive “what-if” fears about infant safety  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia tied to ruminating thoughts  
- Overwhelm with routine tasks; endorses “things getting on top of me”  
- Passive self-harm ideation (no plan/intent): “didn’t want to wake up,” “hospital would be a rest”

Pattern  
All symptom domains cluster in the perinatal period; intensity appears moderate–severe and functionally impairing.

Screening significance  
High clinical concern for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset; co-occurring anxiety/panic symptoms exceed typical “baby blues.”

Risk flags  
- Suicidal ideation (passive) → immediate safety assessment warranted  
- Daily sadness, anhedonia, guilt, anxiety, insomnia → meets DSM threshold indicators for further evaluation  
- Impaired coping with infant care demands → potential impact on bonding and infant safety

Next step  
Recommend urgent psychiatric evaluation and safety planning; consider EPDS formal scoring and referral to perinatal mental health specialty services.
